claim: Yeast spindle pole bodies (SPBs) differentially control the plus-end dynamics and cargoes of their astral microtubules, remotely from the minus-end.
source: Here we show that yeast spindle pole bodies (SPBs, yeast centrosomes) differentially control the plus-end dynamics and cargoes of their astral microtubules, remotely from the minus-end.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript including microscopy images and quantitative analyses.

claim: The old SPB recruits the kinesin motor protein Kip2.
source: The old SPB recruits the kinesin motor protein Kip2, which then translocates to the plus-end of the emanating microtubules, promotes their extension and delivers dynein into the bud.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP accumulation at SPBs and quantification of asymmetric distribution (Figure 4).

claim: Kip2 translocates to the plus-end of emanating microtubules.
source: The old SPB recruits the kinesin motor protein Kip2, which then translocates to the plus-end of the emanating microtubules, promotes their extension and delivers dynein into the bud.
evidence: Demonstrated by kymograph analysis showing Kip2 speckles moving from SPBs to plus-ends (Figure 3a, Video 1).

claim: Kip2 promotes microtubule extension.
source: The old SPB recruits the kinesin motor protein Kip2, which then translocates to the plus-end of the emanating microtubules, promotes their extension and delivers dynein into the bud.
evidence: Supported by published in vitro data and in vivo observations of microtubule length differences (Figure 7b).

claim: Kip2 delivers dynein into the bud.
source: The old SPB recruits the kinesin motor protein Kip2, which then translocates to the plus-end of the emanating microtubules, promotes their extension and delivers dynein into the bud.
evidence: Demonstrated by dynein localization experiments showing asymmetric distribution dependent on Kip2 (Figure 4h-i, Figure 7c-d).

claim: Kip2 recruitment at the SPB depends on Bub2 and Bfa1.
source: Kip2 recruitment at the SPB depends on Bub2 and Bfa1, and phosphorylation of cytoplasmic Kip2 prevents random lattice binding.
evidence: Shown by quantification of Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP in bfa1Δ and bub2Δ mutants showing reduced recruitment (Figure 5a-c).

claim: Phosphorylation of cytoplasmic Kip2 prevents random lattice binding.
source: Kip2 recruitment at the SPB depends on Bub2 and Bfa1, and phosphorylation of cytoplasmic Kip2 prevents random lattice binding.
evidence: Demonstrated by Kip2-S63A mutant showing increased lattice binding and altered distribution profile (Figure 6f-i).

claim: Releasing Kip2 of its control by SPBs equalizes its distribution between the mother cell and its bud.
source: Releasing Kip2 of its control by SPBs equalizes its distribution, the length of microtubules and dynein distribution between the mother cell and its bud.
evidence: Shown by experiments with Kip2-S63A and bfa1Δbub2Δ mutants (Figure 6j-k, Figure 7).

claim: Releasing Kip2 of its control by SPBs equalizes the length of microtubules between the mother cell and its bud.
source: Releasing Kip2 of its control by SPBs equalizes its distribution, the length of microtubules and dynein distribution between the mother cell and its bud.
evidence: Demonstrated by microtubule length measurements in mutants (Figure 7a-b).

claim: Releasing Kip2 of its control by SPBs equalizes dynein distribution between the mother cell and its bud.
source: Releasing Kip2 of its control by SPBs equalizes its distribution, the length of microtubules and dynein distribution between the mother cell and its bud.
evidence: Shown by dynein localization in Kip2-S63A and bfa1Δbub2Δ mutants (Figure 7c-d).

claim: Microtubule organizing centers use minus to plus-end directed remote control to individualize microtubule function.
source: These observations reveal that microtubule organizing centers use minus to plus-end directed remote control to individualize microtubule function.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Microtubule plus-ends explore cellular space by dynamically alternating between periods of growth and shrinkage.
source: The microtubule plus-end grows away from the MTOC and explores the cellular space by dynamically alternating between periods of growth and shrinkage, a process called dynamic instability (Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984).

source: The microtubule plus-end grows away from the MTOC and explores the cellular space by dynamically alternating between periods of growth and shrinkage, a process called dynamic instability (Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984).

claim: Dynamic instability allows microtubules to reach attachment sites such as kinetochores on chromosomes.
source: This search function allows microtubules to reach attachment sites, for example, kinetochores on chromosomes or various cortical sites (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2008; Kirschner and Mitchison, 1986).

claim: All microtubules of a cell are formed from the same pool of tubulin dimers.
source: Remarkably, although all microtubules of a cell are formed from the same pool of tubulin dimers, they can show distinct behaviors and functions.

claim: Microtubules can show distinct behaviors and functions despite being formed from the same pool of tubulin dimers.
source: Remarkably, although all microtubules of a cell are formed from the same pool of tubulin dimers, they can show distinct behaviors and functions.

claim: At least three kinds of microtubules contribute to the assembly of the mitotic spindle in most cell types.
source: For example, in most cell types at least three kinds of microtubules contribute to the assembly of the mitotic spindle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitotic spindle organization.

claim: Different types of microtubules in the mitotic spindle show different lengths and dynamics according to their distinct roles.
source: According to their distinct roles, these microtubules show different lengths and dynamics (Wittmann et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Kinetochore microtubules shrink and pull chromosomes towards the spindle pole.
source: For instance, concomitant to kinetochore microtubules shrinking and pulling chromosomes towards the spindle pole, the interpolar microtubules grow, push the spindle poles away from each other and drive spindle elongation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitotic spindle function.

claim: Interpolar microtubules grow, push the spindle poles away from each other and drive spindle elongation.
source: For instance, concomitant to kinetochore microtubules shrinking and pulling chromosomes towards the spindle pole, the interpolar microtubules grow, push the spindle poles away from each other and drive spindle elongation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitotic spindle function.

claim: Astral microtubules help move the spindle in the cell and position the future cleavage plane.
source: During that time, the astral microtubules that help move the spindle in the cell and position the future cleavage plane, may show different behavior depending on which of the two spindle poles they emanate from (Shaw et al., 1997; Januschke and Gonzalez, 2010; Lengefeld et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Astral microtubules may show different behavior depending on which of the two spindle poles they emanate from.
source: During that time, the astral microtubules that help move the spindle in the cell and position the future cleavage plane, may show different behavior depending on which of the two spindle poles they emanate from (Shaw et al., 1997; Januschke and Gonzalez, 2010; Lengefeld et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Cells have evolved several mechanisms to distinctively control the behavior and function of individual microtubules within a single cellular environment.
source: To distinctively control the behavior and function of individual microtubules even within a single cellular environment, cells have evolved several mechanisms.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the examples that follow in the text.

claim: Microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) can differentially associate with microtubules and contribute to their distinctive behaviors and activities.
source: A diverse set of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs), plus-end tracking proteins (+TIPs), and microtubule-dependent motor proteins can differentially associate with microtubules and contribute to their distinctive behaviors and activities (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Plus-end tracking proteins (+TIPs) can differentially associate with microtubules and contribute to their distinctive behaviors and activities.
source: A diverse set of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs), plus-end tracking proteins (+TIPs), and microtubule-dependent motor proteins can differentially associate with microtubules and contribute to their distinctive behaviors and activities (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Microtubule-dependent motor proteins can differentially associate with microtubules and contribute to their distinctive behaviors and activities.
source: A diverse set of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs), plus-end tracking proteins (+TIPs), and microtubule-dependent motor proteins can differentially associate with microtubules and contribute to their distinctive behaviors and activities (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The behavior of a microtubule often depends on its subcellular environment and the cellular structures that it contacts with its plus-end.
source: In many instances the behavior of a microtubule depends largely on its subcellular environment and the cellular structures that it contacts with its plus-end (capture model; Kirschner and Mitchison, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to the capture model.

claim: Post-translational modifications of tubulin along microtubules modulate both the microtubules' stability and their affinity for regulatory factors in many cell types.
source: Furthermore, in many cell types post-translational modifications of tubulin along microtubules modulate both the microtubules' stability and their affinity for the above regulatory factors (tubulin code; Gadadhar et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on the tubulin code.

claim: In some cells, the behavior of microtubules depends on the MTOC they emanate from.
source: However, in other cells, such as mitotic cells, the behavior of microtubules seems to also depend on the MTOC they emanate from (Januschke and Gonzalez, 2010; Lengefeld et al., 2018; Yamashita et al., 2007; Gasic et al., 2015; and below).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: In many asymmetrically dividing cells one of the two asters forms microtubules that are less dynamic than the other one.
source: For example, in many asymmetrically dividing cells one of the two asters forms microtubules that are less dynamic than the other one.
evidence: This is a general observation supported by citations in the preceding sentence.

claim: How MTOCs specify the plus-end behavior of the microtubules emanating from them remains unknown.
source: However, how MTOCs specify the plus-end behavior of the microtubules emanating from them remains unknown.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the manuscript addresses.

claim: The yeast mitotic spindle assembles within the nucleus between two SPBs embedded in the nuclear envelope.
source: The yeast mitotic spindle assembles within the nucleus between two SPBs embedded in the nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast cell biology.

claim: SPBs nucleate cytoplasmic microtubules that facilitate the movement of the spindle to the mother-bud neck.
source: The SPBs also nucleate cytoplasmic microtubules that facilitate the movement of the spindle to the mother-bud neck and its alignment with the mother-bud axis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast cell biology.

claim: Cytoplasmic microtubules ensure that the mother cell and the bud faithfully inherit each one copy of the genome upon division.
source: Thereby they ensure that the mother cell and the bud faithfully inherit each one copy of the genome upon division.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast cell division.

claim: Throughout yeast preanaphase the two asters of cytoplasmic microtubules are morphologically and functionally distinct.
source: Remarkably, throughout yeast preanaphase the two asters of cytoplasmic microtubules are morphologically and functionally distinct (Shaw et al., 1997; Lengefeld et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The SPB oriented towards the mother cell (m-SPB) is the newly synthesized SPB (young SPB) in virtually all cells.
source: The SPB oriented towards the mother cell (m-SPB), which is the newly synthesized SPB (young SPB) in virtually all cells, nucleates few and short microtubules (m-microtubules).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast SPB age and orientation.

claim: The m-SPB nucleates few and short microtubules (m-microtubules).
source: The SPB oriented towards the mother cell (m-SPB), which is the newly synthesized SPB (young SPB) in virtually all cells, nucleates few and short microtubules (m-microtubules).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature (Shaw et al., 1997; Lengefeld et al., 2018).

claim: The bud-oriented SPB (b-SPB) is inherited from the previous mitosis (old SPB).
source: In contrast, the bud-oriented SPB (b-SPB), which is inherited from the previous mitosis (old SPB), forms long microtubules that extend into the bud (b-microtubules) (Shaw et al., 1997; Lengefeld et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast SPB age and orientation, supported by citations.

claim: The b-SPB forms long microtubules that extend into the bud (b-microtubules).
source: In contrast, the bud-oriented SPB (b-SPB), which is inherited from the previous mitosis (old SPB), forms long microtubules that extend into the bud (b-microtubules) (Shaw et al., 1997; Lengefeld et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The b-microtubules specifically transport the minus-end directed motor protein dynein to their plus-ends.
source: The b-microtubules, specifically, transport the minus-end directed motor protein dynein to their plus-ends and deliver it to the bud cortex (Moore et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: B-microtubules deliver dynein to the bud cortex.
source: The b-microtubules, specifically, transport the minus-end directed motor protein dynein to their plus-ends and deliver it to the bud cortex (Moore et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Dynein at the bud cortex pulls on b-microtubules at anaphase onset.
source: Activated at anaphase onset, dynein at the bud cortex pulls on b-microtubules and facilitates the entry of the b-SPB and the associated daughter nucleus through the bud neck, into the bud (Adames and Cooper, 2000; Tang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Dynein facilitates the entry of the b-SPB and the associated daughter nucleus through the bud neck into the bud.
source: Activated at anaphase onset, dynein at the bud cortex pulls on b-microtubules and facilitates the entry of the b-SPB and the associated daughter nucleus through the bud neck, into the bud (Adames and Cooper, 2000; Tang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: There is no evidence that yeast modifies tubulin along microtubules.
source: Moreover, there is no evidence that yeast modifies tubulin along microtubules (Drummond et al., 2011; Uchimura et al., 2006), indicating that microtubule differentiation inside the cell depends exclusively on the differential recruitment of regulatory proteins.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature showing lack of tubulin modifications in yeast.

claim: Microtubule differentiation in yeast depends exclusively on the differential recruitment of regulatory proteins.
source: Moreover, there is no evidence that yeast modifies tubulin along microtubules (Drummond et al., 2011; Uchimura et al., 2006), indicating that microtubule differentiation inside the cell depends exclusively on the differential recruitment of regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of tubulin modifications in yeast.

claim: Many kinesins regulate microtubule dynamics in addition to their function in cargo transport.
source: Recent work has established that many kinesins, a particularly rich family of microtubule-dependent motor proteins, regulate microtubule dynamics (Howard and Hyman, 2007; Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015) in addition to their function in cargo transport.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Kip3 promotes microtubule catastrophe.
source: While Kip3 promotes microtubule catastrophe (Varga et al., 2006; Arellano-Santoyo et al., 2017; Varga et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2006), that is the switch from plus-end growth to shrinkage, Kip2, which transports dynein to the plus-end of microtubules (Moore et al., 2009), inhibits catastrophe and promotes microtubule elongation (Hibbel et al., 2015; Cottingham and Hoyt, 1997; Huyett et al., 1998; Carvalho et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Catastrophe is the switch from plus-end growth to shrinkage.
source: While Kip3 promotes microtubule catastrophe (Varga et al., 2006; Arellano-Santoyo et al., 2017; Varga et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2006), that is the switch from plus-end growth to shrinkage, Kip2, which transports dynein to the plus-end of microtubules (Moore et al., 2009), inhibits catastrophe and promotes microtubule elongation (Hibbel et al., 2015; Cottingham and Hoyt, 1997; Huyett et al., 1998; Carvalho et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a definition of an established term.

claim: Kip2 transports dynein to the plus-end of microtubules.
source: While Kip3 promotes microtubule catastrophe (Varga et al., 2006; Arellano-Santoyo et al., 2017; Varga et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2006), that is the switch from plus-end growth to shrinkage, Kip2, which transports dynein to the plus-end of microtubules (Moore et al., 2009), inhibits catastrophe and promotes microtubule elongation (Hibbel et al., 2015; Cottingham and Hoyt, 1997; Huyett et al., 1998; Carvalho et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Kip2 inhibits catastrophe.
source: While Kip3 promotes microtubule catastrophe (Varga et al., 2006; Arellano-Santoyo et al., 2017; Varga et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2006), that is the switch from plus-end growth to shrinkage, Kip2, which transports dynein to the plus-end of microtubules (Moore et al., 2009), inhibits catastrophe and promotes microtubule elongation (Hibbel et al., 2015; Cottingham and Hoyt, 1997; Huyett et al., 1998; Carvalho et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Kip2 promotes microtubule elongation.
source: While Kip3 promotes microtubule catastrophe (Varga et al., 2006; Arellano-Santoyo et al., 2017; Varga et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2006), that is the switch from plus-end growth to shrinkage, Kip2, which transports dynein to the plus-end of microtubules (Moore et al., 2009), inhibits catastrophe and promotes microtubule elongation (Hibbel et al., 2015; Cottingham and Hoyt, 1997; Huyett et al., 1998; Carvalho et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Kip3-3xsfGFP intensity increases along cytoplasmic microtubules from minus-ends to plus-ends.
source: In agreement with published in vitro data (Varga et al., 2006; Varga et al., 2009), Kip3-3xsfGFP intensity increased along cytoplasmic microtubules, the protein being barely detectable at their minus-ends and reaching maximal levels at the plus-ends (Figure 1a; note that the abundant GFP fluorescence around the SPB originated from Kip3-3xsfGFP on the nuclear spindle microtubules).
evidence: Demonstrated by line scanning analysis and quantification shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Kip3 amounts at microtubule plus-ends increase linearly with microtubule length.
source: Furthermore, Kip3 amounts at microtubule plus-ends increased linearly with microtubule length (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification and linear regression analysis shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Kip3 is a length-dependent microtubule depolymerase in vivo.
source: Since Kip3 triggers plus-end catastrophes in a manner that depends on the local concentration at the plus-end (Varga et al., 2006; Varga et al., 2009), our analysis indicates that Kip3 is a length-dependent microtubule depolymerase in vivo, consistent with the antenna model established in vitro (Varga et al., 2006; Varga et al., 2009; Gupta et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing length-dependent accumulation and citations to the antenna model.

claim: The distribution of Kip2 follows a different pattern in vivo than Kip3.
source: Strikingly, although in vitro the patterns of Kip2 and Kip3 distribution along microtubules are very similar (Hibbel et al., 2015), the distribution of Kip2 followed a different pattern in vivo: the signal for Kip2-3xsfGFP failed to increase along microtubules.
evidence: Demonstrated by line scanning analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Kip2-3xsfGFP signal remains flat from the minus-end up to the vicinity of the plus-end, where it peaks locally.
source: Instead, it remained flat and above-zero from the minus-end of the microtubule up to the vicinity of its plus-end, where it peaked locally (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Demonstrated by line scanning analysis shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Neither the level of Kip2 along the microtubule nor the height of its plus-end peak varies with microtubule length.
source: Neither the level of the protein along the microtubule nor the height of its plus-end peak varied with microtubule length.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c.

claim: A mechanism distinct from the one suggested in vitro controls Kip2 distribution in living yeast cells.
source: The sharp discrepancy between the distributions of Kip2 in vivo and in vitro suggests that a mechanism distinct from the one suggested in vitro (Hibbel et al., 2015) controls Kip2 distribution in living yeast cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences between in vivo and in vitro distributions.

claim: Kip2 moves processively and at least as fast as Kip3 both in vitro and in vivo.
source: For example, Kip2 moves processively and at least as fast as Kip3, both in vitro (Varga et al., 2006; Varga et al., 2009; Hibbel et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2014) and in vivo (see below and Figure 1—figure supplement 1ab).
evidence: Supported by citations to in vitro studies and reference to in vivo data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1ab.

claim: The mathematical model predicts a flat distribution only in special cases such as when the on-rate is zero or the motor speed is zero.
source: Analytically solving this model predicts a flat distribution only in special cases, such as when the on-rate is zero (no motor on the microtubule lattice) or the motor speed is zero (inactive motors binding everywhere; see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling described in Appendix 1.

claim: The model with static microtubules faithfully represents the flat motor distributions along microtubules of all length categories.
source: Using these estimates, the model with static microtubules faithfully represented the flat motor distributions along microtubules of all length categories (Figure 2b), and we obtained the same qualitative predictions for a model with growing microtubules as a control (see Appendix 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by model fitting shown in Figure 2b and Appendix 1.

claim: The estimated Kip2 concentration and the on-rate constant are close to published values.
source: Importantly, the estimated Kip2 concentration and the on-rate constant were close to published values (Hibbel et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2014) (Figure 2cd, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, see Appendix 1 for details), lending support to the model.
evidence: Model parameter estimates are compared to published values, shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: The median in-rate constant is approximately 500 times higher than the median on-rate constant at each lattice site.
source: Importantly, the median in-rate constant was approximately 500 times higher than the median on-rate constant at each lattice site (p<5∙10−5, see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This is a result from mathematical modeling with statistical significance testing.

claim: Both analytical and numerical modeling results point towards Kip2 initiating its runs predominantly from the microtubule minus-end.
source: Therefore, both the analytical and the numerical modeling results point towards Kip2 initiating its runs on the microtubule predominantly from its minus-end, that is, at or near the SPB from which the microtubule emanates, as an explanation for the unique distribution of Kip2 along microtubules in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mathematical modeling results.

claim: Kip2-3xsfGFP appears as moving speckles along cytoplasmic microtubules.
source: As previously reported (Carvalho et al., 2004), Kip2-3xsfGFP appeared as moving speckles along cytoplasmic microtubules (Video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by time-lapse imaging shown in Video 1 and supported by citation.

claim: Kip2 speckle movement speed in vivo is 6.3 ± 2.1 µm min−1.
source: Kip2 speckle movement speed in these kymographs established that, in vivo, Kip2 runs along microtubules at an average speed of 6.3 ± 2.1 µm min−1 (mean ± S.D., n = 192 speckles, Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), which is more than four times faster than the mean microtubule growth speed under the same conditions (1.4 ± 1.1 µm min−1, mean ± S.D., n = 250 growth phases, Figure 1—figure supplement 1cd).
evidence: Measured from kymographs and quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: Kip2 runs along microtubules more than four times faster than the mean microtubule growth speed.
source: Kip2 speckle movement speed in these kymographs established that, in vivo, Kip2 runs along microtubules at an average speed of 6.3 ± 2.1 µm min−1 (mean ± S.D., n = 192 speckles, Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), which is more than four times faster than the mean microtubule growth speed under the same conditions (1.4 ± 1.1 µm min−1, mean ± S.D., n = 250 growth phases, Figure 1—figure supplement 1cd).
evidence: Calculated from measured speeds shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1cd.

claim: All unambiguous trains of Kip2 motors moving along imaged microtubules started from SPBs and ended at the microtubule plus-ends.
source: Furthermore, in all our experimental Kip2-3xsfGFP kymographs (n = 45), all unambiguous trains of motors (yellow arrowheads, Figure 3a; n = 192) moving along the imaged microtubules started from SPBs and ended at the microtubule plus-ends, as predicted by the model (Figure 3a, Video 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 3a and Video 1.

claim: All fluorescence speckles of Kip2-3xsfGFP analyzed by line scans departed from the SPB, traveled along the microtubule shaft and arrived at the plus-end.
source: As shown in Figure 3b, all the fluorescence speckles that we analyzed this way (n = 9) also departed from the SPB, traveled along the microtubule shaft and arrived at the plus-end.
evidence: Demonstrated by line scan analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Kip3-3xsfGFP rarely appears as fluorescent speckles under the same imaging conditions.
source: In contrast, under the same imaging conditions, Kip3-3xsfGFP rarely appeared as fluorescent speckles (n = 10, from eight kymographs) and the speckles started moving from random places along microtubules (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, Video 2), as expected from Kip3's distribution profile (Figure 1a) and in vitro data (Varga et al., 2006; Varga et al., 2009).
evidence: Demonstrated by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and Video 2.

claim: Kip3 speckles start moving from random places along microtubules.
source: In contrast, under the same imaging conditions, Kip3-3xsfGFP rarely appeared as fluorescent speckles (n = 10, from eight kymographs) and the speckles started moving from random places along microtubules (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, Video 2), as expected from Kip3's distribution profile (Figure 1a) and in vitro data (Varga et al., 2006; Varga et al., 2009).
evidence: Demonstrated by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and Video 2.

claim: The initiation of Kip2 runs is restricted to the minus-ends of microtubules in preanaphase cells.
source: These data support the notion that unlike Kip3, the initiation of Kip2 runs is restricted to the minus-ends of microtubules – at least in preanaphase cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kymograph and line scan analyses.

claim: The ATPase deficient Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP cannot move along the microtubule following its initial binding.
source: The ATPase deficient Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP cannot move along the microtubule following its initial binding and should therefore accumulate at the sites where it is loaded on the microtubules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known requirement of ATP hydrolysis for kinesin movement.

claim: Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP signal accumulates exclusively at one or two point-like structures in preanaphase cells.
source: Strikingly, the Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP signal accumulated exclusively at one or two point-like structures in preanaphase cells and co-expression of the SPB-marker Spc42-mCherry showed that the mutated motor signal systematically localized to or near SPBs (Figure 3c).
evidence: Demonstrated by microscopy imaging shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP systematically localizes to or near SPBs.
source: Strikingly, the Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP signal accumulated exclusively at one or two point-like structures in preanaphase cells and co-expression of the SPB-marker Spc42-mCherry showed that the mutated motor signal systematically localized to or near SPBs (Figure 3c).
evidence: Demonstrated by colocalization with Spc42-mCherry shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP is concentrated on the cytoplasmic side of the SPB.
source: Closer analysis of the signal's distribution indicated that Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP was concentrated on the cytoplasmic side of the SPB.
evidence: This is an observation from detailed analysis of the localization data.

claim: Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP localization extensively overlaps with Spc72-mCherry.
source: Accordingly, Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP localization extensively overlapped with Spc72-mCherry, the receptor of the γ-tubulin complex on the SPB outer-plaque (Knop and Schiebel, 1998) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Kip2 recruitment to microtubules is restricted nearly exclusively to SPBs.
source: This provided further, independent evidence that Kip2 recruitment to microtubules is restricted nearly exclusively to SPBs, that is, at or near the minus-ends of cytoplasmic microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP localization data.

claim: In heterozygous diploid cells expressing both wild type Kip2-mCherry and Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP, the wild type protein decorates microtubule shafts, SPBs and plus-ends.
source: In these cells, the Kip2-mCherry protein decorated microtubule shafts, SPBs and plus-ends, as expected.
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging of heterozygous diploid cells shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In heterozygous diploid cells, the ATPase-deficient mutant Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP remains at or near SPBs.
source: In contrast, the ATPase-deficient, mutant protein remained at or near SPBs (Figure 3d).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging of heterozygous diploid cells shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Very little if any Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP is transported to microtubule plus-ends by the wild type protein.
source: On the opposite, very little if any Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP was transported to microtubule plus-ends by the wild type protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the heterozygous diploid cell imaging shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The heterodimers Kip2/Kip2-G374A are inactive.
source: We conclude that the heterodimers Kip2/Kip2-G374A are inactive and either stay at their loading site on microtubules, like Kip2-G374A homodimers, or rapidly fall off the microtubule shaft.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Kip2-G374A is not transported to plus-ends in heterozygous cells.

claim: The landing of Kip2 on microtubules is highly restricted to SPBs.
source: Moreover, these data established that the landing of Kip2 on microtubules is highly restricted to SPBs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the heterozygous diploid cell experiments.

claim: Kip2 is not directly recruited to microtubule plus-ends, independent of its motor activity.
source: These data also exclude the possibility of Kip2 being directly recruited to microtubule plus-ends, independent of its motor activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Kip2-G374A does not accumulate at plus-ends.

claim: The two SPBs of preanaphase cells do not recruit equal levels of Kip2.
source: Strikingly, quantification of the GFP signal in cells coexpressing Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP and Spc42-mCherry established that the two SPBs of preanaphase cells did not recruit equal levels of Kip2.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: b-SPBs accumulate approximately four times more Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP than m-SPBs.
source: b-SPBs localized near the bud neck accumulated approximately four times more of the ATPase-deficient Kip2 variant than m-SPBs (Figure 4ab).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: In the vast majority of yeast cells, the b-SPB is the SPB inherited from the previous mitosis (old SPB).
source: In the vast majority of yeast cells, the b-SPB is the SPB inherited from the previous mitosis (old SPB), whereas the m-SPB is newly synthesized (Pereira et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast SPB age and orientation, supported by citation.

claim: Spc42-mCherry can differentiate SPBs by age since Spc42 proteins in old SPBs carry mature mCherry compared with immature mCherry in new SPBs.
source: Spc42-mCherry can differentiate SPBs by age since Spc42 proteins in old SPBs carry mature – and thus reliably brighter – mCherry compared with immature mCherry in new SPBs (Lengefeld et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a method for distinguishing SPB age, supported by citation.

claim: The asymmetry of Kip2-G374A-3xfsGFP is much stronger in cells with correct SPB orientation than in cells with inverted SPBs.
source: When we separated the cells that correctly oriented the old SPB towards the bud from those few ones (6%) that inverted the orientation of their SPBs, we noticed that the asymmetry of Kip2-G374A-3xfsGFP was much stronger in cells with correct orientation (Figure 4a).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4a-c.

claim: In cells with correctly oriented SPBs, the median asymmetry index value for Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP is 0.7.
source: In about 94% of the cells, the SPBs are correctly oriented: their b-SPB is the old one and the median asymmetry index value is 0.7 (Figure 4c).
evidence: Quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: In cells with inverted SPB orientation, Kip2-G374A-3xfsGFP is significantly biased towards the old SPB.
source: Strikingly, also in cells with inverted SPB orientation, Kip2-G374A-3xfsGFP was significantly biased towards the old SPB, the m-SPB in this case.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4c.

claim: In cells with inverted SPBs, the median asymmetry index value for Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP is −0.2.
source: In these cells, asymmetry was less pronounced (median asymmetry index value: −0.2) than in cells with correct orientation, suggesting that some spatial information biased the recruitment of Kip2 towards the b-SPB as well.
evidence: Quantified from experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Both the age of the SPB and the vicinity to the bud-neck synergistically activate SPBs for Kip2 recruitment.
source: In cells with correctly oriented SPBs, the strong bias of Kip2 recruitment towards the b-SPB would then result from the effects of both the age and location of SPBs. We concluded that both the age of the SPB and the vicinity to the bud-neck synergistically activate SPBs for Kip2 recruitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of correctly oriented and inverted SPB cells.

claim: Kip2 levels are nearly two-fold higher at the plus-ends of b-microtubules than of m-microtubules in cells that carry a cytoplasmic microtubule on both sides of the spindle.
source: In the few cells that carry a cytoplasmic microtubule on both sides of the spindle, Kip2 levels were nearly two-fold higher at the plus-ends of b-microtubules than of m-microtubules (Figure 4de).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 4d-e.

claim: The asymmetry index of Kip2-3xsfGFP on microtubule plus-ends shows the same pattern as for Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP on SPBs.
source: The asymmetry index of Kip2-3xsfGFP on microtubule plus-ends in cells with cytoplasmic microtubules emanating from both SPBs showed the same pattern as for Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP on SPBs (Figure 4df).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison of asymmetry indices shown in Figure 4d-f.

claim: SPBs are the main determinants for Kip2 recruitment to microtubules.
source: These data further supported the idea that SPBs are the main determinants for Kip2 recruitment to microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation between Kip2 levels at SPBs and at microtubule plus-ends.

claim: The b-SPB grows microtubules on average twice as long as those emanating from the m-SPB.
source: Indeed, the b-SPB, which recruits Kip2 more actively, causes the emanating microtubules to carry more Kip2, and on average grows microtubules twice as long as those emanating from the m-SPB (Figure 4g).
evidence: Demonstrated by microtubule length measurements shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The increased loading of Kip2 on b-microtubules correlates well with the localization of dynein.
source: Likewise, the increased loading of Kip2 on b-microtubules correlates well with the localization of dynein, one of the known cargos of Kip2 (Carvalho et al., 2004; Caudron et al., 2008; Markus et al., 2009; Figure 4h).
evidence: Demonstrated by dynein localization shown in Figure 4h and supported by citations.

claim: Dynein levels at microtubule plus-ends are strongly decreased in kip2∆ mutant cells.
source: Supporting the idea that dynein localization depends on Kip2 distribution, dynein levels at microtubule plus-ends were strongly decreased in kip2∆ mutant cells (Carvalho et al., 2004; Caudron et al., 2008; Markus et al., 2009 and Figure 4h), and dynein was restricted to SPBs in the Kip2-G374A mutant cells (Figure 4h).
evidence: Demonstrated by dynein localization in mutants shown in Figure 4h and supported by citations.

claim: Dynein is restricted to SPBs in Kip2-G374A mutant cells.
source: Supporting the idea that dynein localization depends on Kip2 distribution, dynein levels at microtubule plus-ends were strongly decreased in kip2∆ mutant cells (Carvalho et al., 2004; Caudron et al., 2008; Markus et al., 2009 and Figure 4h), and dynein was restricted to SPBs in the Kip2-G374A mutant cells (Figure 4h).
evidence: Demonstrated by dynein localization shown in Figure 4h.

claim: Dynein distribution shows the same correlation with old SPBs as Kip2.
source: Furthermore, dynein distribution showed the same correlation with old SPBs as Kip2, being most asymmetric in cells with correctly oriented SPBs, and slightly asymmetric towards the old SPB when SPBs were inverted (Figure 4i).
evidence: Demonstrated by dynein asymmetry quantification shown in Figure 4i.

claim: SPB-dependent recruitment of Kip2 to microtubules might be one of the mechanisms through which yeast cells promote the growth of b-microtubules and bias dynein distribution towards them.
source: Thus, SPB-dependent recruitment of Kip2 to microtubules might be one of the mechanisms through which yeast cells promote the growth of b-microtubules and bias dynein distribution towards them.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlations between Kip2 recruitment, microtubule length, and dynein distribution.

claim: Bub2 and Bfa1 function together as a bipartite GTPase-activating protein (GAP) complex for the GTPase Tem1.
source: The SPB-associated proteins Bub2 and Bfa1 function together as a bipartite GTPase-activating protein (GAP) complex for the GTPase Tem1 and partly independently of each other in SPB specification.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Bub2 and Bfa1 function.

claim: In early preanaphase, Bub2 and Bfa1 are recruited to the old SPB upon its specification by the Spindle Pole Inheritance Network (SPIN).
source: In early preanaphase, they are recruited to the old SPB upon its specification by the Spindle Pole Inheritance Network (SPIN).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Bub2 and Bfa1 localization.

claim: When the SPB moves to the vicinity of the bud neck later in preanaphase, Bub2 and Bfa1 levels are further enhanced by the position of the SPB.
source: When the SPB moves to the vicinity of the bud neck later in preanaphase, the levels are further enhanced by the position of the SPB.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Bub2 and Bfa1 regulation.

claim: Bub2 and Bfa1 are most strongly biased to the old SPB when this SPB is the b-SPB compared to when it is the m-SPB.
source: As a consequence, they are most strongly biased to the old SPB when this SPB is the b-SPB compared to when it is the m-SPB (Lengefeld et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: In anaphase cells, Bub2 and Bfa1 accumulate to high levels on the b-SPB as it enters the bud, irrespective of the SPB's age.
source: In anaphase cells, Bub2 and Bfa1 accumulate to high levels on the b-SPB as it enters the bud, irrespective of the SPB's age (Bardin et al., 2000; Pereira et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The pattern of Bub2 and Bfa1 distribution is highly reminiscent of that of Kip2.
source: Therefore, the pattern of Bub2 and Bfa1 distribution is highly reminiscent of that of Kip2.
evidence: This is an observation based on comparing the known distributions of Bub2/Bfa1 and Kip2.

claim: Either bfa1∆ or bub2∆ single deletions or the bfa1∆ bub2∆ double deletion lowers the levels of Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP on the b-SPB almost by half.
source: Either of these single or double deletions lowered the levels of Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP on the b-SPB almost by half, while the Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP signal on the m-SPB was unchanged (Figure 5ab).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: bfa1∆ and bub2∆ deletions do not affect the Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP signal on the m-SPB.
source: Either of these single or double deletions lowered the levels of Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP on the b-SPB almost by half, while the Kip2-G374A-3xsfGFP signal on the m-SPB was unchanged (Figure 5ab).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: bfa1 and bub2 deletions make SPB orientation more random.
source: The deletions had the known effect of making the SPB orientation more random (Lengefeld et al., 2017 and Figure 5c).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5c and supported by citation.

claim: Compared to wild type cells, the asymmetry of ATPase deficient Kip2 is strongly reduced on properly oriented SPBs in bfa1∆ bub2∆ mutants.
source: The asymmetry index indicated that cells with properly oriented and inverted SPBs now behaved very similarly: compared to wild type cells, the asymmetry of ATPase deficient Kip2 was strongly reduced on properly oriented SPBs and fully erased on inverted SPBs (Figure 5c).
evidence: Demonstrated by asymmetry index quantification shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The asymmetry of ATPase deficient Kip2 is fully erased on inverted SPBs in bfa1∆ bub2∆ mutants.
source: The asymmetry index indicated that cells with properly oriented and inverted SPBs now behaved very similarly: compared to wild type cells, the asymmetry of ATPase deficient Kip2 was strongly reduced on properly oriented SPBs and fully erased on inverted SPBs (Figure 5c).
evidence: Demonstrated by asymmetry index quantification shown in Figure 5c.

claim: bfa1 and bub2 deletions do not affect the pattern of Kip2 distribution along microtubule shafts.
source: Importantly, bfa1 and bub2 deletions did not affect the pattern of Kip2 distribution along microtubule shafts, which remained flat, peaking only at the plus-ends, independent of microtubule length (Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by line scanning analysis shown in Figure 5d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The median in-rate constant (kin) is 12 times lower in the bub2∆ bfa1∆ double mutant than in wild type cells.
source: The median in-rate constant (recruitment rate at the minus-end, kin) was 12 times lower in the bub2∆ bfa1∆ double mutant than in wild type cells (Figure 5e, p=0.0008 when assuming a Kip2 concentration of ≥ 35 nM, Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3abc, see Appendix1 for details), while the median on-rate constant (kon) was not significantly reduced.
evidence: Demonstrated by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The median on-rate constant (kon) is not significantly reduced in the bub2∆ bfa1∆ double mutant.
source: The median in-rate constant (recruitment rate at the minus-end, kin) was 12 times lower in the bub2∆ bfa1∆ double mutant than in wild type cells (Figure 5e, p=0.0008 when assuming a Kip2 concentration of ≥ 35 nM, Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3abc, see Appendix1 for details), while the median on-rate constant (kon) was not significantly reduced.
evidence: Demonstrated by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 5e.

claim: In cells lacking Bub2 and Bfa1, the initiation of Kip2 runs is still restricted to SPBs but is reduced on the b-SPB to the level observed on the m-SPB.
source: Together, these data indicated that in cells lacking Bub2 and Bfa1, the initiation of Kip2 runs was still restricted to SPBs but was reduced on the b-SPB to the level observed on the m-SPB.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling and quantification data in bfa1∆ bub2∆ mutants.

claim: In all bfa1∆ and bub2∆ single and double mutant cells, Kip2-3xsfGFP levels drop at the plus-ends of b-microtubules to nearly m-microtubule levels.
source: Indeed, in all bfa1∆ and bub2∆ single and double mutant cells Kip2-3xsfGFP levels dropped at the plus-ends of b-microtubules to nearly m-microtubule levels, while remaining unchanged at the plus-ends of m-microtubules, compared to wild type cells (Figure 5f).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Kip2-3xsfGFP levels remain unchanged at the plus-ends of m-microtubules in bfa1∆ and bub2∆ mutants compared to wild type cells.
source: Indeed, in all bfa1∆ and bub2∆ single and double mutant cells Kip2-3xsfGFP levels dropped at the plus-ends of b-microtubules to nearly m-microtubule levels, while remaining unchanged at the plus-ends of m-microtubules, compared to wild type cells (Figure 5f).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Kip2-3xsfGFP levels at the plus-ends of microtubules are more symmetric in bfa1∆ and bub2∆ mutants.
source: Consistently, Kip2-3xsfGFP levels at the plus-ends of microtubules in cells with both cytoplasmic microtubules were now more symmetric (Figure 5g and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by asymmetry index quantification shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Bub2 and Bfa1 contribute together to Kip2 recruitment on the b-SPB and to the enhanced rate of Kip2 run initiation on b-microtubules.
source: Hence, Bub2 and Bfa1, which respond synergistically to historical and spatial cues to accumulate specifically on the b-SPB, contribute together to Kip2 recruitment on the b-SPB and to the enhanced rate of Kip2 run initiation on b-microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the effects of bfa1 and bub2 deletions on Kip2 distribution.

claim: Kip2's N-terminus is heavily phosphorylated in vivo in a GSK3-, Cdk1-, and Dbf2/20-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, Kip2's N-terminus is heavily phosphorylated in vivo in a GSK3-, Cdk1-, and Dbf2/20-dependent manner (Drechsler et al., 2015) (Figure 6a); the kinases Dbf2 and Dbf20 function in the yeast Hippo pathway (Hergovich et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature and shown schematically in Figure 6a.

claim: GSK3-dependent phosphorylation is primed through phosphorylation of serine 63.
source: GSK3-dependent phosphorylation is primed through phosphorylation of serine 63, which is conserved across Kip2 orthologues in fungi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and falls into a consensus site for the mitotic kinases Cdk1 and Dbf2/20.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Serine 63 is conserved across Kip2 orthologues in fungi.
source: GSK3-dependent phosphorylation is primed through phosphorylation of serine 63, which is conserved across Kip2 orthologues in fungi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and falls into a consensus site for the mitotic kinases Cdk1 and Dbf2/20.
evidence: Demonstrated by sequence alignment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphorylation of the N-terminus of Kip2 inhibits Kip2 binding to microtubules.
source: Furthermore, phosphorylation of the N-terminus of Kip2 inhibits Kip2 binding to microtubules (Drechsler et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Mutation of S63 to alanine (KIP2-S63A) largely reduces Kip2 phosphorylation.
source: As reported (Drechsler et al., 2015), mutation of S63 to alanine (KIP2-S63A) largely reduced Kip2 phosphorylation (Figure 6b).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot shown in Figure 6b and supported by citation.

claim: Both SPBs recruit more of the hypo-phosphorylated, ATPase deficient protein Kip2-S63A-G374A-3xsfGFP.
source: Interestingly, both SPBs recruited more of the hypo-phosphorylated, ATPase deficient protein Kip2-S63A-G374A-3xsfGFP (Figure 6cd) but this recruitment was still asymmetric between SPBs, except in cells with inverted SPB orientation (Figure 6e).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 6c-e.

claim: Kip2-S63A-G374A-3xsfGFP recruitment is still asymmetric between SPBs, except in cells with inverted SPB orientation.
source: Interestingly, both SPBs recruited more of the hypo-phosphorylated, ATPase deficient protein Kip2-S63A-G374A-3xsfGFP (Figure 6cd) but this recruitment was still asymmetric between SPBs, except in cells with inverted SPB orientation (Figure 6e).
evidence: Demonstrated by asymmetry index quantification shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Preventing Kip2 phosphorylation does not affect much the role of the SPBs in Kip2 recruitment.
source: Thus, preventing Kip2 phosphorylation did not affect much the role of the SPBs in Kip2 recruitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Kip2-S63A-G374A still shows asymmetric recruitment.

claim: The distribution profile of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP along microtubules deviates strongly from that of Kip2-3xsfGFP and resembles more that of Kip3.
source: In contrast, the distribution profile of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP along microtubules deviated strongly from that of Kip2-3xsfGFP and resembled more that of Kip3 (Figure 1a): The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP linearly increased from the minus- to the plus-ends of the microtubules, and plus-end levels increased with microtubule length (Figure 6f, Video 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by line scanning analysis shown in Figure 6f and Video 3.

claim: The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP linearly increase from the minus- to the plus-ends of the microtubules.
source: In contrast, the distribution profile of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP along microtubules deviated strongly from that of Kip2-3xsfGFP and resembled more that of Kip3 (Figure 1a): The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP linearly increased from the minus- to the plus-ends of the microtubules, and plus-end levels increased with microtubule length (Figure 6f, Video 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by line scanning analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Plus-end levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP increase with microtubule length.
source: In contrast, the distribution profile of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP along microtubules deviated strongly from that of Kip2-3xsfGFP and resembled more that of Kip3 (Figure 1a): The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP linearly increased from the minus- to the plus-ends of the microtubules, and plus-end levels increased with microtubule length (Figure 6f, Video 3).
evidence: Demonstrated by line scanning analysis shown in Figure 6f.

claim: The median on-rate constant of Kip2-S63A (kon) is significantly higher than for the wild type protein.
source: These estimates indicate that the median on-rate constant of Kip2-S63A (kon) is significantly higher than for the wild type protein (p<2∙10−4 when assuming a Kip2 concentration of ≥ 35 nM, Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3abd, see Supplemental information for details), while the median in-rate constant (kin, minus-end recruitment) is not significantly changed (Figure 6g).
evidence: Demonstrated by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 6g.

claim: The median in-rate constant (kin, minus-end recruitment) is not significantly changed in Kip2-S63A.
source: These estimates indicate that the median on-rate constant of Kip2-S63A (kon) is significantly higher than for the wild type protein (p<2∙10−4 when assuming a Kip2 concentration of ≥ 35 nM, Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3abd, see Supplemental information for details), while the median in-rate constant (kin, minus-end recruitment) is not significantly changed (Figure 6g).
evidence: Demonstrated by mathematical modeling shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Phosphorylation of Kip2's N-terminus primarily inhibits Kip2 from landing on microtubules.
source: These estimates indicate that phosphorylation of Kip2's N-terminus primarily inhibits Kip2 from landing on microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results showing increased on-rate in Kip2-S63A.

claim: The hypo-phosphorylated, ATPase-deficient Kip2-S63A-G374A-3xsfGFP protein decorates both microtubule shafts and SPBs in heterozygous diploid cells co-expressing Kip2-mCherry.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the hypo-phosphorylated, ATPase-deficient Kip2-S63A-G374A-3xsfGFP protein decorated both microtubule shafts and SPBs in heterozygous diploid cells co-expressing Kip2-mCherry (Figure 6hi).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging shown in Figure 6h-i.

claim: The Kip2-S63A mutation largely bypasses the differential control of Kip2 recruitment to microtubules exerted by SPBs.
source: Furthermore, the Kip2-S63A mutation largely bypassed the differential control of Kip2 recruitment to microtubules exerted by SPBs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that Kip2-S63A shows more symmetric distribution.

claim: The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP on plus-ends increase on both m- and b-microtubules.
source: The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP on plus-ends increased on both m- and b-microtubules, and the level differences between them were substantially reduced compared to wild type (Figure 6j and Figure 4e).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 6j.

claim: The level differences of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP between m- and b-microtubules are substantially reduced compared to wild type.
source: The levels of Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP on plus-ends increased on both m- and b-microtubules, and the level differences between them were substantially reduced compared to wild type (Figure 6j and Figure 4e).
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification shown in Figure 6j.

claim: The asymmetry of hypo-phosphorylated Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP levels between m- and b-microtubule plus-ends is reduced and no-longer depends on whether the spindle is properly oriented or not.
source: Moreover, the asymmetry of hypo-phosphorylated Kip2-S63A-3xsfGFP levels between m- and b-microtubule plus-ends was reduced and no-longer depended on whether the spindle was properly oriented or not (Figure 6k and Figure 4f).
evidence: Demonstrated by asymmetry index quantification shown in Figure 6k.

claim: Preventing Kip2 landing along microtubules is a pre-requisite for the control of Kip2 recruitment by SPBs.
source: Therefore, preventing Kip2 landing along microtubules is a pre-requisite for the control of Kip2 recruitment by SPBs and Kip2 phosphorylation is key in this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the effects of the Kip2-S63A mutation.

claim: Kip2 phosphorylation is key in preventing Kip2 landing along microtubules.
source: Therefore, preventing Kip2 landing along microtubules is a pre-requisite for the control of Kip2 recruitment by SPBs and Kip2 phosphorylation is key in this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the effects of the Kip2-S63A mutation.

claim: Neither Kip2 phosphorylation nor Bub2 and Bfa1 control the differential rate of microtubule nucleation between m- and b-SPBs by themselves.
source: This remained true in the KIP2-S63A, bub1∆, bfa1∆ single and the bub2∆ bfa1∆ double mutant strains (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b), indicating that neither Kip2 phosphorylation nor Bub2 and Bfa1 control the differential rate of microtubule nucleation between m- and b-SPBs by themselves.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that most preanaphase cells do not form measurable m-microtubules in these mutants.

claim: Kip2 hypo-phosphorylation (KIP2-S63A mutant cells) causes both m- and b-microtubules to become longer on average compared to wild type cells.
source: Kip2 hypo-phosphorylation (KIP2-S63A mutant cells) caused both m- and b-microtubules to become longer on average compared to wild type cells (Figure 7ab), in agreement with these microtubules carrying higher levels of the microtubule polymerizing kinesin Kip2 at their plus-ends (Figure 6j and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by microtubule length measurements shown in Figure 7a-b.

claim: In KIP2-S63A mutant cells, the m- and b-microtubules are no-longer significantly different in length.
source: In these mutant cells, the m- and b-microtubules were no-longer significantly different in length.
evidence: Demonstrated by microtubule length measurements shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Inactivation of Bfa1, Bub2, or both eliminates the length difference between m- and b-microtubules by reducing the average length of b- to that of m-microtubules.
source: Inactivation of Bfa1, Bub2, or both also eliminated the length difference between m- and b-microtubules, but in this case by reducing the average length of b- to that of m-microtubules (Figure 7ab).
evidence: Demonstrated by microtubule length measurements shown in Figure 7a-b.

claim: The KIP2-S63A, bfa1∆, bub2∆, and bfa1∆ bub2∆ mutations randomize dynein distribution in cells carrying both b- and m- microtubules.
source: Consistent with these effects, the KIP2-S63A, bfa1∆, bub2∆, and bfa1∆ bub2∆ mutations randomized dynein distribution in cells carrying both b- and m- microtubules (Figure 7cd).
evidence: Demonstrated by dynein localization and asymmetry quantification shown in Figure 7c-d.

claim: In KIP2-S63A, bfa1∆, bub2∆, and bfa1∆ bub2∆ mutant cells, Dyn1-mNeonGreen localizes indistinguishably to the tip of both b- and m-microtubules.
source: Unlike in wild type cells, Dyn1-mNeonGreen localized indistinguishably to the tip of both b- and m-microtubules in all these mutant cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by dynein localization shown in Figure 7c-d.

claim: Restricting the initiation of Kip2 runs to the b-SPBs functions as a molecular determinant for specifying the length and function of b-microtubules in vivo.
source: We therefore concluded that restricting the initiation of Kip2 runs to the b-SPBs functioned as a molecular determinant for specifying the length and function of b-microtubules in vivo.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the effects of mutations affecting Kip2 recruitment on microtubule length and dynein distribution.

claim: The remote-control mechanism for patterning microtubule organization and function relies on a dedicated mode of kinesin regulation.
source: Here, we identify a remote-control mechanism for patterning microtubule organization and function at the subcellular level in yeast and demonstrate that this mechanism relies on a dedicated mode of kinesin regulation (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarized in Figure 7e.

claim: The cytoplasmic pool of the kinesin is inhibited in its ability to bind microtubules at random positions.
source: This process relies on two main conditions: the cytoplasmic pool of the kinesin is inhibited in its ability to bind microtubules at random positions, and at least one MTOC provides activities promoting the recruitment and reactivation of the kinesin locally, at the minus-end of the microtubule.
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated by the effects of Kip2 phosphorylation.

claim: At least one MTOC provides activities promoting the recruitment and reactivation of the kinesin locally, at the minus-end of the microtubule.
source: This process relies on two main conditions: the cytoplasmic pool of the kinesin is inhibited in its ability to bind microtubules at random positions, and at least one MTOC provides activities promoting the recruitment and reactivation of the kinesin locally, at the minus-end of the microtubule.
evidence: This is a key finding demonstrated by the role of Bub2/Bfa1 and SPB-dependent recruitment.

claim: Releasing the specificity of the SPB or the cytoplasmic inhibition of the kinesin equalizes the distribution of the kinesin and its cargoes, and prevents microtubule differentiation.
source: Releasing the specificity of the SPB or the cytoplasmic inhibition of the kinesin equalizes the distribution of the kinesin and its cargoes, and prevents microtubule differentiation.
evidence: Demonstrated by the effects of Kip2-S63A and bfa1∆bub2∆ mutations.

claim: In budding yeast, the remote-control of microtubule plus-ends by the SPBs is a major mechanism for establishing spindle asymmetry and differentiating the behavior of selected microtubules.
source: Thus, at least in budding yeast, the remote-control of microtubule plus-ends by the SPBs is a major mechanism for establishing spindle asymmetry and differentiating the behavior of selected microtubules.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Modification of the kinesin rather than of microtubules prevents cytoplasmic Kip2 from landing at random locations along microtubules.
source: Interestingly, modification of the kinesin rather than of microtubules prevented cytoplasmic Kip2 from landing at random locations along microtubules.
evidence: This is a key finding about the mechanism of Kip2 regulation.

claim: Landing-inhibition of Kip2 is achieved through phosphorylation.
source: Landing-inhibition was achieved through phosphorylation, probably the simplest mechanism possible.
evidence: Demonstrated by the effects of the Kip2-S63A mutation.

claim: Phosphorylation involves a domain of Kip2 with many potential phosphorylation sites, most of which are targeted by yeast GSK3-related kinases.
source: Remarkably, phosphorylation involves a domain of Kip2 with many potential phosphorylation sites, most of which are targeted by yeast GSK3-related kinases (Drechsler et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Once initiated by the priming kinase, Gsk3 can very efficiently maintain Kip2 in a highly phosphorylated state.
source: Once initiated by the priming kinase, Gsk3 can very efficiently maintain Kip2 in a highly phosphorylated state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism of GSK3 action.

claim: Preventing Kip2 phosphorylation does not slow down its release from microtubule tips (kout).
source: Interestingly, preventing Kip2 phosphorylation did not slow down its release from microtubule tips (kout), indicating that even if Kip2 phosphorylation took place at microtubule tips, it is not the determining step for releasing the kinesin.
evidence: This is an inference from the modeling results showing unchanged kout in Kip2-S63A.

claim: Kip2 phosphorylation specifically prevents reloading of cytoplasmic Kip2 to random places on microtubules and thereby ensures the supremacy of SPBs in the control of Kip2 recruitment.
source: Thus, Kip2 phosphorylation specifically prevents reloading of cytoplasmic Kip2 to random places on microtubules and thereby ensures the supremacy of SPBs in the control of Kip2 recruitment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the effects of Kip2 phosphorylation.

claim: Kip2 recruitment activity at SPBs most likely requires high-affinity or many low-affinity binding sites for phosphorylated Kip2 at the MTOC.
source: As a consequence, Kip2 recruitment activity at SPBs most likely requires two components. First, a high-affinity or many low-affinity binding sites for phosphorylated Kip2 must be present at the MTOC to ensure its recruitment against competing binding sites on microtubules: even if phosphorylated Kip2 binds them only poorly, the surface of the microtubules in the cell and the number of tubulin dimers that they expose is orders of magnitude greater than the size of the microtubule minus-end.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the need to compete with microtubule binding sites.

claim: At SPBs the kinesin must be released of the inhibition that prevents its binding to the microtubule lattice.
source: Second, at SPBs the kinesin must be released of the inhibition that prevents its binding to the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the need for Kip2 to bind microtubules to walk along them.

claim: An as yet unidentified phosphatase locally activates Kip2 at SPBs.
source: This suggests that an as yet unidentified phosphatase locally activates Kip2 at SPBs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the need to reverse phosphorylation-mediated inhibition.

claim: The remote-control model of microtubule behavior by MTOCs is conserved beyond yeast.
source: We suggest that the remote-control model of microtubule behavior by MTOCs as identified here is conserved beyond yeast and might even provide a useful perspective for solving open issues of how the tubulin code is established and maintained in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculation based on similarities in other organisms.

claim: The remote-control model might provide a useful perspective for solving open issues of how the tubulin code is established and maintained in vivo.
source: We suggest that the remote-control model of microtubule behavior by MTOCs as identified here is conserved beyond yeast and might even provide a useful perspective for solving open issues of how the tubulin code is established and maintained in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential broader implications.

claim: The recruitment of specific kinesins by MTOCs could be a mechanism for controlling the recruitment of tubulin modifiers.
source: We propose that the recruitment of specific kinesins by MTOCs could be a mechanism for controlling the recruitment of tubulin modifiers.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Recent data in mammalian cells indicate that kinesins control at least some microtubule modifications such as acetylation.
source: Indeed, recent data in mammalian cells indicate that kinesins control at least some microtubule modifications such as acetylation (Tang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Microtubule longevity is a prerequisite for the acquisition of many tubulin modifications.
source: In addition, microtubule longevity is a prerequisite for the acquisition of many tubulin modifications (Roll-Mecak, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Microtubule-stabilizing messenger kinesins such as Kip2 are excellent candidates for modulating the propensity of microtubules to acquire specific modifications.
source: Therefore, microtubule-stabilizing messenger kinesins such as Kip2 are excellent candidates for modulating the propensity of microtubules to acquire specific modifications.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of Kip2 in stabilizing microtubules.

claim: MTOC asymmetry can precede asymmetric tubulin modification and microtubule spatial orientation in the meiotic spindle.
source: In that regard, we note that MTOC asymmetry can precede asymmetric tubulin modification and microtubule spatial orientation in the meiotic spindle (Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: At least some tubulin modifiers are actually kinesin cargos.
source: Finally, it is tempting to speculate that at least some tubulin modifiers are actually kinesin cargos.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: Yeast cells are not the only asymmetrically dividing cells that form asters of different sizes during mitosis.
source: Indeed, yeast cells are not the only asymmetrically dividing cells that form asters of different sizes during mitosis. The one cell embryo of C. elegans, Drosophila neuroblasts and male germline stem cells show similar asymmetries (Januschke and Gonzalez, 2010; Yamashita et al., 2007; Grill et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on other organisms.

claim: Centrosomes segregate non-randomly and as a function of their age in many stem cells, from fruit fly to the mouse.
source: Furthermore, centrosomes segregate non-randomly and as a function of their age in many stem cells, from fruit fly to the mouse (Lengefeld and Barral, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to review literature.

claim: In many cell-types the centrosomes seem to be able to control the plus-end dynamics and functions of the microtubules that they nucleate, depending on centrosome age.
source: Thus, in many cell-types the centrosomes seem to be able to control the plus-end dynamics and functions of the microtubules that they nucleate, depending on centrosome age.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observations in various organisms.

claim: At least a few kinesins feature the critical ability to lose the ability to bind and walk along microtubules when phosphorylated in organisms as distant from yeast as metazoans.
source: Furthermore, at least a few kinesins feature the critical ability to lose the ability to bind and walk along microtubules when phosphorylated in organisms as distant from yeast as metazoans (Kevenaar et al., 2016; Kelliher et al., 2018; Drerup et al., 2016); this supports the notion that kinesins can function as messengers between MTOCs and microtubule plus ends in many eukaryotes.
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on metazoan kinesins.

claim: Kinesins can function as messengers between MTOCs and microtubule plus ends in many eukaryotes.
source: Furthermore, at least a few kinesins feature the critical ability to lose the ability to bind and walk along microtubules when phosphorylated in organisms as distant from yeast as metazoans (Kevenaar et al., 2016; Kelliher et al., 2018; Drerup et al., 2016); this supports the notion that kinesins can function as messengers between MTOCs and microtubule plus ends in many eukaryotes.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations showing conservation of the mechanism.

claim: Not all kinesins are regulated by MTOCs.
source: Finally, it is clear that not all kinesins are regulated by MTOCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the contrasting behaviors of Kip2 and Kip3.

claim: Cytoplasmic microtubules in preanaphase yeast cells are decorated in a SPB-independent but length-dependent manner by Kip3.
source: As we show for preanaphase yeast cells, cytoplasmic microtubules are decorated in a SPB-independent but length-dependent manner by a microtubule-destabilizing kinesin-8 (Kip3), and concomitantly in a SPB-dependent but length-independent manner by a microtubule-stabilizing kinesin-7 (Kip2).
evidence: Demonstrated by the distribution analyses shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cytoplasmic microtubules in preanaphase yeast cells are decorated in a SPB-dependent but length-independent manner by Kip2.
source: As we show for preanaphase yeast cells, cytoplasmic microtubules are decorated in a SPB-independent but length-dependent manner by a microtubule-destabilizing kinesin-8 (Kip3), and concomitantly in a SPB-dependent but length-independent manner by a microtubule-stabilizing kinesin-7 (Kip2).
evidence: Demonstrated by the distribution analyses shown in Figure 1.

claim: The fission yeast S. pombe homologs of Kip2 (Tea2) and Kip3 (Klp5/6) exhibit a similar pattern of kinesin accumulation at microtubule plus-ends.
source: The fission yeast S. pombe homologs of Kip2 (Tea2) and Kip3 (Klp5/6) were recently shown to exhibit a similar pattern of kinesin accumulation at microtubule plus-ends (Meadows et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: The two distinct but co-existing modes of kinesin recruitment likely underlie microtubule stability control by kinesin competition at microtubule plus ends.
source: The two distinct but co-existing modes of kinesin recruitment likely underlies microtubule stability control by kinesin competition at microtubule plus ends (Meadows et al., 2018), leading to a complex balance of regulation on different microtubules.
evidence: Supported by citation and inference from the data.

claim: The control of kinesin distribution emerges as a code in itself that has distinct and predictable effects on the function and dynamics of the underlying microtubules.
source: Thus, the control of kinesin distribution emerges here as a code in itself that has distinct and predictable effects on the function and dynamics of the underlying microtubules, as well as on the patterning of cellular microtubule organization.
evidence: This is a main conclusion of the study.
